Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The fiery leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah militant movement assured Lebanon on Monday that his movement will cooperate in the country's political life. Supporters carry posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah. Hassan Nasrallah said: "We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone." Nasrallah spoke a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman the country's president after a six-month vacancy in the position. Nasrallah, speaking at a packed stadium, told his followers: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese." He said Sleiman's election "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start." "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs, we are both in front of two choices; either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon and we prefer the second choice." The parliament had tried 19 times to vote on a new president, but failed because of disagreements over how to share power in a new Cabinet. Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a deal last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that pushed the country to the brink of civil war, and paved the way for Sleiman's election. The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government in which the Cabinet would be comprised of 30 posts -- 16 for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition and three set aside for the president to nominate. The seat allocation had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure it had the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power. In exchange for the veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest that has paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006. In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and to the Arab League for helping broker the deal. Sleiman was the consensus candidate, and is viewed as a neutral party by Lebanon's political factions. The nation's previous presidents have been seen as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. In his 10 years as chief of the army, Sleiman also is believed to have unified the splintered military. However, he inherits a nation grappling with divisions. Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah. In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, triggering fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region. The election helped end a political crisis that deteriorated into violence this month. That crisis was defused when the Lebanese government gave in to two key Hezbollah demands -- lifting a government ban of Hezbollah's telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport. "The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah said. "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares - and unfortunately we must speak of shares - even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah's shares." Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli, and other Western targets and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. But many in Lebanon and other parts of the Middle East -- particularly Shiites -- view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** — The prominent leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah movement assured the nation on Monday that his group is committed to constructive participation in the country's political life. Addressing a packed stadium where supporters waved posters bearing his image, Hassan Nasrallah declared: "We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone."

Nasrallah’s address came a day after the Lebanese parliament elected Michel Sleiman as president, ending a six-month power vacuum at the head of state. Speaking to the crowd, Nasrallah stated: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese." He added that Sleiman's election "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start."

Acknowledging the severe domestic fractures, Nasrallah noted: "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs, we are both in front of two choices; either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon and we prefer the second choice."

Parliament had previously convened 19 times in failed attempts to elect a new president, consistently deadlocked over power-sharing arrangements in a new Cabinet. The breakthrough occurred last week when Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a landmark agreement aimed at resolving an 18-month political crisis that had pushed the country to the brink of civil war, ultimately paving the way for Sleiman's election.

Brokered in Doha, Qatar, the accord establishes a 30-seat consensus Cabinet, allocating 16 posts to the parliamentary majority, 11 to the Hezbollah-led opposition, and three to be nominated by the president. The seat distribution was a key point of contention for the opposition, which demanded sufficient representation to veto major executive decisions—a power secured by obtaining 11 seats. In exchange for veto power and electoral redistricting ahead of next year’s polls, Hezbollah agreed to dismantle the sit-in protest that had paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006.

In his address, President Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and the Arab League for brokering the deal. Sleiman emerged as a consensus candidate viewed as a neutral figure by Lebanon's competing political factions, standing in contrast to previous presidents who were seen as decidedly pro-Syrian or pro-Western. Having unified a fractured military during his decade as army chief, Sleiman nonetheless inherits a nation grappling with deep political divisions. 

Lebanon's elected, Western-backed government has long been locked in a bitter power struggle with Hezbollah. Through public statements and street demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah had threatened to leverage its strength and popularity to bring down the Sunni-led government, raising fears of a renewed civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region.

The presidential election helped defuse a crisis that had escalated into violent clashes earlier this month. Tensions eased only after the government conceded to two central Hezbollah demands: rescinding a ban on Hezbollah's private telecommunications network and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's international airport.

"The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah asserted. "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares - and unfortunately we must speak of shares - even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah's shares."

While the United States designates Hezbollah as a terrorist organization due to its history of attacks against American, Israeli, and Western targets, many in Lebanon and across the Middle East—particularly within the Shiite community—view its fighters as a legitimate resistance movement.

**Title:** From the Brink of War to National Unity: The 2008 Doha Accord and the Reshaping of Lebanese Politics

### Introduction
In May 2008, Lebanon stood at its most dangerous crossroads since the end of its devastating 1975–1990 civil war. An 18-month political paralysis had left the country without a head of state, paralyzed its democratic institutions, and ultimately spilled over into violent street clashes. The deadlock pitted the Western- and Saudi-backed governing coalition against an opposition alliance led by the Iranian- and Syrian-backed militant and political group Hezbollah. Just as the nation seemed on the verge of collapsing into renewed sectarian conflict, intense diplomatic mediation in Doha, Qatar, yielded a landmark power-sharing agreement. The accord not only resolved the presidential vacancy with the election of General Michel Sleiman but also inaugurated a fragile era of national unity marked by public pledges of political cooperation from Hezbollah’s leadership.

---

### The Anatomy of an 18-Month Crisis
The roots of the 2008 crisis lay in the profound geopolitical and domestic divisions that followed the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri. By late 2006, the political landscape was polarized into two main blocs: 
1. **The March 14 Alliance:** The pro-Western governing majority led by Prime Minister Fouad Siniora and Saad Hariri, advocating for state sovereignty and the disarming of militias.
2. **The March 8 Coalition:** The opposition led by Hezbollah and the Free Patriotic Movement, demanding a veto-yielding share of the cabinet and maintaining that Hezbollah's military arm was essential for national defense against Israel.

The crisis intensified in November 2006 when six opposition ministers resigned from the cabinet, rendering the government contested in the eyes of the opposition. When President Émile Lahoud’s term expired in November 2007, Parliament failed to achieve the necessary quorum to elect a successor. For six months, the presidency remained vacant, the government operated under a cloud of dubious legitimacy, and parliamentary sessions were repeatedly boycotted.

The political stalemate turned deadly in early May 2008. After the Siniora government moved to shut down Hezbollah’s private fiber-optic telecommunications network and fire the head of security at Beirut Airport (a Hezbollah ally), Hezbollah viewed the decisions as a declaration of war. In a swift display of force, Hezbollah and its allies took control of West Beirut, engaging in fierce street battles with pro-government gunmen. Dozens of people were killed, exposing the extreme fragility of the Lebanese state.

---

### The Doha Negotiations: Brokering a Breakthrough
Fearing a full-scale descent into civil war, an emergency Arab League ministerial committee—led by the State of Qatar and its Prime Minister, Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani—intervened. The committee managed to secure a ceasefire in Beirut and persuaded leaders from across Lebanon’s political spectrum to gather in Doha for crisis talks.

After six days of grueling negotiations under the auspices of the Amir of Qatar, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, the warring factions reached a comprehensive deal on May 21, 2008, known as the **Doha Agreement**. 

The agreement rested on four major pillars:
1. **The Election of a Neutral President:** Immediate consensus on Army Commander General Michel Sleiman as a compromise candidate to fill the vacant presidency.
2. **A National Unity Government:** The formation of a 30-seat cabinet structured to grant the opposition 11 seats—giving them the "blocking third" (veto power) they had long demanded—while the parliamentary majority held 16 seats and the president appointed 3 neutral ministers.
3. **Electoral Reform:** The adoption of a revised electoral law based on smaller, 1960-era districts for the upcoming 2009 parliamentary elections, satisfying long-held Christian opposition demands.
4. **Security Guarantees:** A strict ban on the use of weapons or armed violence to resolve internal political disputes.

---

### Implementation: Sleiman’s Election and Nasrallah’s Pledge
The impact of the Doha Accord was immediate. On May 25, 2008, the Lebanese Parliament convened in a historic session attended by foreign dignitaries, Arab leaders, and European diplomats. MPs officially elected General Michel Sleiman as the 12th President of the Lebanese Republic, ending the half-year presidential vacuum.

In his inaugural address, President Sleiman emphasized national reconciliation, the strengthening of state institutions, and the need for a unified national defense strategy that defined the relationship between the state armed forces and Hezbollah's resistance.

Crucially, the agreement received public endorsement from Hezbollah’s Secretary-General, Hassan Nasrallah. In a major address following the summit, Nasrallah welcomed the election of Sleiman and pledged Hezbollah’s full political collaboration in building a national unity government. He framed the Doha Accord not as a victory for one faction over another, but as a triumph for all of Lebanon, committing his movement to resolving future grievances solely through political dialogue rather than armed force.

---

### Legacy and Aftermath
The Doha Agreement was widely hailed as a masterclass in regional diplomacy. It successfully pulled Lebanon back from the precipice of civil war, restored functional governance, and paved the way for peaceful parliamentary elections in 2009. 

While the accord did not permanently eliminate the deep-seated structural and geopolitical tensions in Lebanon, it served as a vital circuit breaker. By establishing a framework for compromise and power-sharing, the Doha Accord demonstrated that even in the face of profound sectarian divisions, political consensus remained the only viable path toward maintaining Lebanese stability and national unity.

counterfactuals.output:
**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** — Hezbollah leader Sheikh Hassan Nasrallah struck a reconciliatory tone Monday, welcoming the election of Lebanon's new president and declaring a "new page" for the nation following a deep political crisis that brought the country to the brink of a new civil war.

Speaking via video link to thousands of cheering supporters in southern Beirut, Nasrallah pledged to work with President Michel Sleiman, the former army chief who was sworn in Sunday as part of a Qatar-brokered deal aimed at ending an 18-month political paralysis.

"Today we announce the start of a new stage, a stage of national unity, cooperation, and partnership," Nasrallah told the crowd gathered to mark Liberation Day, which commemorates the 2000 withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.

Nasrallah praised Sleiman’s inaugural address, in which the new president called for a national dialogue to address Hezbollah’s controversial weapons arsenal and formulate a cohesive national defense strategy.

"We endorse the president's call for dialogue, and we are ready to discuss a national defense strategy that protects Lebanon from Israeli aggression," Nasrallah said. 

The Hezbollah chief sought to reassure political rivals that his group’s powerful armed wing would not be used to achieve domestic political gains—an issue that had boiled over just weeks earlier when Hezbollah fighters briefly seized control of West Beirut in violent clashes that left dozens dead.

"These weapons are not intended for internal use," Nasrallah insisted, reiterating his movement's stance that the May violence was a necessary response to government decisions that threatened Hezbollah’s private communications network. "The weapons of the resistance are to fight the enemy, to liberate our land, and to defend Lebanon."

The election of Sleiman filled a presidential vacuum that had persisted since November 2007, when former President Emile Lahoud stepped down without a successor. The resulting deadlock between the U.S.-backed, pro-government coalition led by Prime Minister Fouad Siniora and the Iran- and Syria-backed opposition led by Hezbollah brought state institutions to a virtual standstill.

The crisis culminated earlier this month in the worst sectarian fighting Lebanon had seen since the end of its 1975–1990 civil war. 

Arab League mediators intervened, leading to the Doha Agreement last week. Under the deal, opposition forces were granted veto power over cabinet decisions, a long-standing demand of Hezbollah and its allies, paving the way for Sleiman's election.

Western leaders, including U.S. President George W. Bush and French President Nicolas Sarkozy, congratulated Sleiman on his election, expressing hope that his presidency would usher in stability and strengthen Lebanese sovereignty.

However, analysts note that major hurdles remain for the country. Sleiman faces the immediate challenge of overseeing the formation of a national unity cabinet, a process historically fraught with political maneuvering and delays in Lebanon's complex power-sharing system. 

Despite the looming challenges, Nasrallah urged his followers and political opponents alike to embrace the compromise reached in Qatar.

"Lebanon cannot be governed by one faction or one group," Nasrallah said. "Lebanon can only survive through consensus and unity."

**THE INTERNATIONAL HERALD & DIPLOMATIC REVIEW**  
**SPECIAL REPORT**

**BREAKTHROUGH IN DOHA: LEBANESE FACTIONS SIGN LANDMARK ACCORD TO END 18-MONTH POLITICAL CRISIS**

**DOHA, Qatar / BEIRUT, Lebanon** — In a dramatic diplomatic breakthrough mediated by the Arab League, opposing Lebanese political factions signed a comprehensive peace accord in Qatar, bringing a swift end to an 18-month political paralysis that had brought Lebanon to the brink of a disastrous new civil war. 

The deal, dubbed the **Doha Agreement**, was reached after six days of intensive, round-the-clock negotiations led by Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani and Emir Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani. The accord resolves a dangerous power vacuum that had left Lebanon without a president since November 2007 and sparked horrific street violence earlier in the month.

---

### **Context: From Deadlock to the Brink of War**

The political crisis began in late 2006 when opposition ministers—primarily from the Shiite parties Hezbollah and Amal—resigned from the Western-backed cabinet of Prime Minister Fouad Siniora. The opposition demanded a "national unity" government with veto power, which the ruling March 14 coalition refused to grant. 

The impasse erupted into an armed conflict in early May 2008 when the Siniora government attempted to dismantle Hezbollah’s private fiber-optic telecommunications network and remove the head of airport security, an official sympathetic to the group. 

Reacting swiftly and forcefully, Hezbollah and its allies launched a military operation in West Beirut, overrunning Sunni neighborhoods loyal to the government, shutting down pro-government media outlets, and defeating allied militias in a matter of days. The violent display demonstrated Hezbollah’s domestic military dominance and forced the government to rescind its decisions, setting the stage for the emergency talks in Qatar.

---

### **Key Terms of the Doha Agreement**

The agreement addresses the core constitutional, political, and security grievances that fed the 18-month crisis:

1. **Election of a Consensus President:**  
   The factions agreed to immediately convene Parliament to elect General Michel Suleiman, Commander of the Lebanese Armed Forces, as President of the Republic. Suleiman is viewed as a neutral figure capable of bridging the gap between rival blocs.

2. **Formation of a National Unity Government (The "Blocking Third"):**  
   The agreement reshuffles the 30-member Cabinet to give the Hezbollah-led opposition its long-demanded veto power. The cabinet will be divided as follows:
   * **16 seats** for the majority coalition (March 14).
   * **11 seats** for the opposition (March 8), providing them with the minimum seats required to veto cabinet decisions (a "blocking third").
   * **3 seats** to be directly appointed by the neutral President.

3. **New Electoral Law for 2009:**  
   The sides agreed to adopt a modified version of the 1960 electoral law, dividing the country into smaller electoral districts (particularly in Beirut). This change was a key demand of General Michel Aoun, Hezbollah’s main Christian ally, who argued it would ensure fair representation for Christian voters in the upcoming 2009 parliamentary elections.

4. **Prohibition of Arms for Political Leverage:**  
   The signatory parties explicitly pledged not to use weapons or security infrastructure to settle political disputes, acknowledging the traumatic events of early May. 

5. **Re-establishment of State Authority and National Dialogue:**  
   The accord dictates an end to all forms of civil disobedience, including the long-standing protest encampment that had paralyzed downtown Beirut for over a year. Furthermore, the parties agreed that the new President would launch a comprehensive National Dialogue to discuss strengthening state authority and formulating a national defense strategy (a euphemism for addressing Hezbollah’s arsenal).

---

### **Hezbollah’s Reaction: A Claim of Strategic Victory**

Hezbollah and its leadership reacted to the signing of the Doha Agreement with triumphant rhetoric, framing the compromise as a decisive victory for the "Resistance" and its political vision. 

* **Validation of Demands:** Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah praised the agreement, noting that the political opposition had secured its primary long-term goal: guaranteed veto power (the blocking third) over all major government decisions. 
* **Defense of its Arsenal:** Hezbollah successfully navigated the talks without surrendering its weapons. While the agreement prohibited the internal use of arms, Hezbollah maintained that its arsenal remained dedicated solely to deterring Israeli aggression. The group reiterated that its military action in May was a defensive move to protect the "infrastructure of the Resistance" (the communications network) against what it termed government "aggression."
* **Immediate De-escalation:** Following the agreement, Hezbollah and its allies immediately moved to dismantle their tent city in downtown Beirut and dismantled roadblocks leading to Beirut International Airport, allowing normal life to return to the capital.

Analysts note that Hezbollah emerged from the crisis as the undisputed dominant power in Lebanon—demonstrating both its ability to project decisive military power domestically and its ability to translate that military leverage into constitutional political gains.

---

### **International and Domestic Reactions**

* **Beirut:** Citizens took to the streets in celebrations, firing celebratory gunshots and setting off fireworks. While relief was palpable, underlying tensions remained high following the violence of previous weeks. Prime Minister Fouad Siniora welcomed the deal, expressing hope that it would inaugurate a new era of stability, though members of his coalition privately lamented having to concede cabinet veto power under the threat of arms.
* **The Arab World:** Qatari Emir Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani declared, "There are no victors and no vanquished in this deal. The only winner is Lebanon." Syria and Iran, Hezbollah's primary foreign patrons, promptly endorsed the accord.
* **The West:** The United States and France issued cautious endorsements. US officials welcomed the resolution of the presidency and the end of violence, but expressed deep concern over Hezbollah’s enhanced political leverage and the unresolved issue of its armed wing.

---

### **Conclusion and Outlook**

The Doha Agreement successfully pulled Lebanon back from the edge of catastrophe, restoring state institutions and providing a temporary roadmap for political stability. However, while the immediate structural crisis has been resolved through the election of General Suleiman and the creation of a national unity government, deep political divisions remain. 

The ultimate test for Lebanon will be whether the state can maintain stability as it navigates the upcoming 2009 parliamentary elections, and whether the planned National Dialogue can realistically address the fundamental question of Hezbollah’s weapons within a sovereign state.

**BEIRUT** — Hezbollah leader Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah has called for a new era of “national partnership” in Lebanon, extending a tentative olive branch following the parliamentary election of General Michel Sleiman as president and the signing of a landmark accord aimed at pulling the country back from the brink of civil war.

Speaking in a televised address broadcast across the capital, Nasrallah welcomed the election of Sleiman, the former chief of the Lebanese Armed Forces, framing it as a vital victory for national unity. The Hezbollah chief insisted that no single political bloc could govern the deeply divided nation alone. 

“Lebanon cannot be built, nor can its sovereignty be protected, except through cooperation, integration, and national partnership,” Nasrallah told thousands of supporters watching on large screens in Beirut’s southern suburbs. “We must turn the page on the past and move forward with a spirit of reconciliation.”

Nasrallah’s remarks come just days after Lebanese leaders concluded an intense, Qatari-brokered summit in Doha, which halted an eighteen-month political stalemate that had paralyzed the nation's institutions and repeatedly erupted into violence.

### The 30-Seat Formula and Veto Power

Central to the Doha Agreement is a power-sharing arrangement for a new 30-seat cabinet, a compromise designed to satisfy both the Western-backed parliamentary majority and the opposition led by Hezbollah.

Under the agreed formula:
* **16 seats** will be allocated to the ruling March 14 coalition, led by Saad Hariri.
* **11 seats** will go to the March 8 opposition, granting Hezbollah and its allies the crucial "blocking third"—a veto power over major cabinet decisions that they had demanded for over a year.
* **3 seats** will be appointed directly by President Sleiman, positioning him as an independent arbiter between the two rival blocs.

The allocation effectively grants the opposition the constitutional power to block major decisions and prevent the government from collapsing, a key concession that the majority coalition had long resisted. 

### Shadow of Recent Violence

The call for partnership follows the most severe internal violence Lebanon has witnessed since the end of the 1975–1990 civil war. 

Earlier this month, street fighting paralyzed Beirut after the government of Prime Minister Fouad Siniora moved to dismantle Hezbollah’s private fiber-optic telecommunications network and reassign the chief of airport security, who was seen as close to the militant group. 

In a swift and overwhelming show of strength, armed Hezbollah fighters and their allies seized control of large swathes of Sunni-dominated West Beirut, routing pro-government militias in a matter of hours. The clashes, which quickly spread to the Chouf mountains and northern Lebanon, left more than 80 people dead and threatened to reignite full-scale sectarian conflict between Shiite, Sunni, and Druze communities.

The escalation forced the government to rescind its decrees, paving the way for the emergency talks in Qatar that ultimately produced the political deal and cleared the path for Sleiman’s ascension to the presidency—a post that had remained vacant since November.

### A Fragile Peace Ahead

President Sleiman, a 59-year-old career military officer, earned broad respect for keeping the army neutral during the recent clashes and the preceding political crisis. In his inaugural address to parliament, Sleiman emphasized the need for national dialogue, specifically addressing the sensitive issue of Hezbollah’s arsenal—a topic that remains the central fault line in Lebanese politics.

While Nasrallah praised Sleiman’s posture toward the "resistance" against Israel, Western diplomats and local analysts remain cautious. They note that while the Doha Agreement and the 30-seat cabinet formula have successfully contained the immediate political fire, the underlying ideological divides—and the question of who holds a monopoly on weapons in Lebanon—remain far from resolved.

For now, however, residents in Beirut express a cautious sense of relief. As the new administration prepares to navigate the complex process of cabinet formation, the streets of the capital have returned to a fragile calm, trading the crackle of gunfire for the cautious rhetoric of political compromise.

**Nasrallah Calls for Unity After Presidential Election, Defends Hezbollah’s Arsenal**

**BEIRUT** — One day after Lebanon’s parliament elected Army Chief Gen. Michel Suleiman as president, Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah delivered a televised address calling for a "new era" of national reconciliation, while fiercely defending his group’s right to maintain its military arsenal.

Speaking via video link to thousands of supporters gathered in Beirut’s southern suburbs to mark "Resistance and Liberation Day"—the annual anniversary of Israel’s 2000 withdrawal from southern Lebanon—Nasrallah praised the election of Suleiman as a victory for national unity. 

However, the Hezbollah leader made clear that the Iranian-backed militant group and political party had no intention of disarming, framing its weapons as vital to defending Lebanon against Israel.

### Context: Weeks of Violence Lead to Doha Deal

Nasrallah’s speech followed one of the most dangerous escalations in Lebanon since the end of its 1975–1990 civil war. 

The political crisis reached a breaking point in early May 2008, when the Western-backed government of Prime Minister Fouad Siniora took steps to dismantle Hezbollah’s private fiber-optic telecommunications network and remove the head of airport security over alleged ties to the group. 

Viewing the move as a declaration of war against its military apparatus, Hezbollah and its allies launched a swift armed takeover of Sunni-dominated areas in West Beirut. The sectarian fighting quickly spread to the Shouf mountains and northern regions, leaving more than 80 people dead and pushing the country to the brink of a new civil war.

The violent street clashes forced the government to back down, leading to Qatar-brokered negotiations in Doha. On May 21, Lebanese political factions signed the Doha Agreement. The deal ended an 18-month political stalemate, granting Hezbollah and its allies veto power in a new cabinet, agreeing on a new electoral law, and paving the way for the long-delayed election of Gen. Suleiman to fill the presidency, which had been vacant since November 2007.

### Nasrallah Reaffirms Stance on Weapons and Reconciliation

In his May 26 address, Nasrallah struck a dual tone of compromise and defiance. He welcomed President Suleiman’s inaugural speech, in which the newly elected chief of state advocated for a national defense strategy that would utilize Hezbollah's capabilities alongside the Lebanese Armed Forces.

Addressing the controversial decision to turn Hezbollah’s weapons against internal rivals earlier in the month, Nasrallah insisted the action was a legitimate defense of the resistance's infrastructure. He claimed that the government's attempt to shut down Hezbollah's communications network was orchestrated by foreign powers—specifically the United States—to disarm the movement.

"We did not seek to use our weapons internally," Nasrallah declared, arguing that the May 7 armed response was designed to protect the resistance from being compromised. He pledged that Hezbollah's weapons would never be used to seek political power or alter the domestic balance of force, provided the government did not target the group's network again.

"The weapons of the resistance are to fight the enemy, liberate occupied land, and protect Lebanon," Nasrallah said, urging all political factions to put the recent bloodshed behind them and focus on forming a national unity government.

### Reaction and Outlook

While Hezbollah supporters celebrated the speech as a confirmation of their group's strategic victory, members of the ruling pro-Western "March 14" coalition remained skeptical. Critics pointed out that despite Nasrallah's assurances, Hezbollah had demonstrated its willingness to use force domestically to achieve political objectives, altering the dynamics of Lebanese governance.

Despite the lingering tensions, the immediate threat of widespread violence appeared to recede. The election of Suleiman and Nasrallah’s speech marked a tense return to political dialogue in Lebanon, though fundamental disagreements regarding the status of Hezbollah’s weapons and the country's foreign alignment remain unresolved.

**BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** -- Hezbollah leader Sheikh Hassan Nasrallah offered explicit assurances of political cooperation to Lebanon’s newly elected president on Monday, declaring a willingness to work toward national unity following a landmark power-sharing deal that ended an 18-month political stalemate.

Speaking via video link to thousands of supporters gathered in Beirut’s southern suburbs, Nasrallah welcomed the election of former army chief Gen. Michel Sleiman, who was sworn in by parliament on Sunday to fill a presidential vacuum that had dragged on since November.

"We look forward to working together in a spirit of cooperation and partnership to build a strong, capable, and unified state," Nasrallah said during the televised address. "Today, we open a new page in Lebanon’s history."

Nasrallah specifically endorsed the national dialogue vision outlined by Sleiman in his inaugural address, which touched on a strategy for national defense and the status of Hezbollah’s weapons. 

"The president's speech expressed the consensus of all Lebanese, and we support his call for a national defense strategy that protects the country," Nasrallah stated, reiterating that his movement’s vast military arsenal would never be turned inward against fellow Lebanese citizens. 

The political breakthrough was made possible by a Qatar-brokered compromise reached last week in Doha, which halted a dangerous escalation of sectarian violence that saw Hezbollah fighters briefly seize control of Sunni neighborhoods in West Beirut.

Central to the Doha agreement is a crucial power-sharing formula for a new 30-member cabinet. Under the terms of the deal, the U.S.-backed parliamentary majority will hold 16 seats, the Hezbollah-led opposition will receive 11 seats, and President Sleiman will appoint the remaining three ministers. 

By securing 11 seats, the opposition gains a blocking minority—or veto power—over major executive decisions, fulfilling a long-standing demand that had paralyzed Lebanese politics and brought the nation to the brink of another civil war.

The political resolution highlights the starkly divided perception of Hezbollah on the international stage versus its standing at home. 

In the United States, Israel, and much of the Western world, Hezbollah is officially designated as a foreign terrorist organization, condemned for its past attacks on Western targets, its commitment to Israel's destruction, and its heavy financial and military backing from Iran and Syria. 

However, within Lebanon and across large swathes of the Middle East, Hezbollah maintains a vastly different image. To its supporters, the Shia movement operates not only as a legitimate and highly organized political party represented in parliament, but also as a vital social welfare provider and a heroic "resistance" force. Many in the region credit Hezbollah with ending Israel’s 18-year occupation of southern Lebanon in 2000 and praise its performance during the 34-day war with Israel in the summer of 2006.

While Nasrallah’s conciliatory tone has lowered political temperatures in Beirut, significant hurdles lie ahead. President Sleiman faces the daunting task of forming a cabinet alongside designated Prime Minister Fouad Siniora and launching a national dialogue to tackle long-term issues, chief among them the controversial role of Hezbollah's arms within the sovereign state.
